entities.summary:
Friar Antonio Sancho de Benevento (died 1600) stands as a prominent silversmith artist of the Spanish Renaissance, whose ecclesiastical vocation as a Hieronymite monk at the Monastery of Sant Jeroni de Cotalba, near Gandia (Valencia), profoundly shaped his artistic output. Flourishing in the late 16th century, his work exemplifies the intricate fusion of religious devotion and humanistic artistic principles characteristic of the period, particularly within the Kingdom of Valencia. His contributions extended beyond mere craftsmanship, influencing the aesthetic and material culture of the Valencian nobility and clergy through his exquisite liturgical and decorative commissions.

His most celebrated achievement is the monumental silver altarpiece for the high altar of Sant Jeroni de Cotalba, a project that occupied him for decades until his death in 1600. This masterwork, though now lost, was renowned for its intricate relief work, depicting biblical scenes and figures with a blend of late Gothic precision and burgeoning Renaissance naturalism. Benevento also contributed significantly to the monastery's treasury and chapel adornments, creating processional crosses, reliquaries, and chalices that were highly prized. His artistic process often involved collaboration with other artisans, synthesizing various techniques and materials to achieve a harmonious, spiritually resonant aesthetic.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Antonio Sancho de Benevento significantly shaped the material culture and artistic standards of ecclesiastical silversmithing in the Kingdom of Valencia, particularly through his monumental altarpiece at Sant Jeroni de Cotalba. His work exemplified the fusion of monastic devotion and Renaissance artistry, leaving an enduring, albeit mostly lost, legacy on regional artistic production.
